Until the 1840s, a message could travel no faster than the horse, ship or train that carried it. The electric telegraph changed that almost overnight. By sending pulses of current along a wire, operators could transmit messages across great distances in a matter of minutes, using a code of short and long signals. Within a few decades, telegraph lines stretched across continents, and in 1866 a cable laid across the floor of the Atlantic finally linked Europe and North America after several earlier attempts had failed. The consequences were profound. Newspapers could report events from distant countries on the day they happened, governments could communicate instantly with their representatives abroad, and traders could compare prices in different markets. Not everyone was impressed. Some commentators complained that the flood of brief, unconfirmed reports encouraged superficial thinking, while others worried that private messages could be read by operators. Telegraph companies also charged by the word, which led customers to develop a famously abbreviated style of writing. In many respects, these debates closely resemble those surrounding the digital technologies of our own time.

questions.passage: Dyes were among the most precious commodities of the ancient world. The deep purple prized by Roman emperors, for instance, was extracted from sea snails, and thousands of them were needed to colour a single garment, making it a symbol of wealth and power. For centuries, all dyes came from plants, animals or minerals, and many colours remained expensive or faded quickly. This changed in 1856, when an eighteen-year-old English chemistry student named William Perkin was attempting to produce an artificial version of quinine, a medicine used against malaria. His experiment failed, but while cleaning his equipment he noticed that the dark residue produced a brilliant purple colour when dissolved in alcohol. Realising its commercial potential, Perkin left his studies, patented the substance and opened a factory to manufacture it. The new colour, known as mauve, became extremely fashionable, and its success inspired chemists across Europe to search for other synthetic dyes. The industry that grew from these efforts went on to produce not only colours but also medicines, perfumes and explosives. Perkin's accidental discovery is therefore often regarded as a turning point in the history of the chemical industry.

Pigments were made from minerals such as iron oxide and charcoal, and some were probably blown onto the walls through hollow bones. Researchers believe this happens partly because musical memories are stored in areas of the brain that tend to be damaged later in the disease than those responsible for other kinds of memory. In recent years, programmes offering personalised playlists to people with dementia have spread across care homes in several countries. Studies suggest that listening to familiar music can reduce agitation and anxiety, and in some cases lessen the need for sedative drugs. Group singing sessions appear to bring additional benefits, encouraging social contact and giving carers a different way of connecting with the people they look after. Scientists are careful, though, not to exaggerate what music can do. There is no convincing evidence that it slows the progress of the disease itself, and its effects often fade soon after the music stops. Nevertheless, given its low cost and lack of side effects, many experts believe it deserves a far more central place in care.

Weeks later, he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the child remained healthy. Such an experiment would be considered completely unethical today. Nearly two centuries later, in 1980, smallpox became the first human disease to be officially declared eradicated.

questions.passage: Every flat map of the world is, in some sense, a compromise. Its great advantage was that a line of constant compass direction appeared on the map as a straight line, making it far easier to plot a course across the ocean. The price of this convenience was a dramatic distortion of size towards the poles. On a Mercator map, Greenland appears roughly as large as Africa, although Africa is in reality about fourteen times bigger. For centuries, this did not matter greatly, since the map was used mainly for navigation. However, as it became the standard image of the world in schools and offices, some critics argued that it gave a misleading impression, making Europe and North America look larger and more important than they really are. Several alternative projections have been proposed that show areas more accurately, although they inevitably distort shapes instead. Many online map services still use a version of Mercator's projection, because it preserves the shapes of streets and buildings when users zoom in.

He suspected that the electricity was produced by the contact between the two metals, with the frog merely acting as a conductor. The disagreement between the two scientists became one of the most famous scientific debates of the age. To prove his theory, Volta built a tall stack of alternating discs of zinc and copper, separated by pieces of cardboard soaked in salt water. When the top and bottom of the pile were connected by a wire, it produced a steady electric current. Announced in 1800, this 'voltaic pile' was the first battery, and it allowed scientists to study electricity in a way that had previously been impossible. Within weeks, researchers had used it to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. As it turned out, both men were partly right: Volta's explanation of the battery was correct, but nerves and muscles do indeed use electrical signals. The unit of electrical potential, the volt, is named in his honour.

Sociologists attribute this shift to several factors, including the influence of celebrities and athletes, improvements in hygiene and technique, and a growing emphasis on self-expression. For many wearers, a tattoo marks a significant life event, commemorates a loved one or expresses an identity they wish to make visible. Attitudes in the workplace have changed more slowly. Although many employers now accept visible tattoos, surveys suggest that some recruiters, particularly in customer-facing or traditional professions, still view them negatively. As a result, a number of people choose designs that can easily be covered by clothing. The popularity of tattoos has also fuelled demand for their removal. Laser treatment has become more effective, but it remains expensive, often painful and may require many sessions over a period of months. Dermatologists advise those considering a tattoo to think carefully about its location and design, since tastes that seem permanent at twenty may look very different at fifty.

statements.text: Tattoos were once linked to a limited range of social groups.

questions.passage: Is chess a sport? The question may sound frivolous, but it has practical consequences, since recognition as a sport can bring access to public funding, inclusion in multi-sport events and tax advantages for clubs. The International Olympic Committee recognised chess as a sport many years ago, although it has never been included in the Olympic Games themselves. Supporters of the classification emphasise the demands of top-level competition. Elite players prepare physically as well as mentally, since games can last for several hours and require intense concentration throughout. Studies have even recorded elevated heart rates and substantial energy use among players during important tournaments. Sceptics respond that physical activity is surely central to the definition of a sport, and that if chess qualifies, so too might card games or crossword competitions. Meanwhile, the game itself has experienced a remarkable surge in popularity. Online platforms allow millions of people to play at any hour against opponents around the world, and a popular television drama about a fictional chess prodigy prompted a sharp increase in sales of chess sets. Live broadcasts of top players, accompanied by expert commentary, now attract audiences comparable to those of some traditional sports.

statements.text: Chess has been played at the Olympic Games.
Top chess players may prepare physically for competitions.

questions.passage: Every Saturday morning, in parks across many countries, thousands of people gather to run, jog or walk a five-kilometre course. The events are free, organised entirely by volunteers and open to anyone, regardless of age or ability. Participants register once, receive a personal barcode and can then take part as often as they like, receiving their time by message later the same day. What began as a small gathering of friends in a single park has grown into a global movement involving millions of registered participants. Its appeal lies partly in its inclusiveness. Unlike organised races, which can be expensive and intimidating for beginners, the weekly runs place no emphasis on winning, and many events deliberately include a volunteer who walks at the back to ensure that nobody finishes last alone. Health researchers have taken a keen interest, since the events appear to attract many people who previously did little exercise. Surveys of participants report improvements not only in fitness but also in mental well-being and feelings of belonging to a community. Interestingly, some people take part exclusively as volunteers, marshalling the course or recording times, and say they gain similar social benefits without running at all.

questions.passage: Women's football has a longer history than many people realise. In the early twentieth century, some women's matches in Britain attracted crowds of tens of thousands, until the national football association banned women from playing on its members' grounds, a restriction that remained in place for half a century. In recent years, however, the women's game has grown at an extraordinary pace. International tournaments now fill large stadiums, broadcast audiences have reached record levels and sponsors who once showed little interest are competing for deals. The increase in visibility has had a noticeable effect on participation, with many more girls joining clubs and school teams. Yet considerable inequalities remain. Outside the top leagues, many professional players earn modest salaries and combine football with other jobs, and facilities, medical support and coaching are often inferior to those available to men. Researchers have also pointed out that much sports science, including the design of boots and approaches to injury prevention, has been based on male athletes, which may help to explain why certain injuries appear more common among women. Campaigners argue that sustained investment, rather than occasional enthusiasm around major tournaments, is essential if the recent progress is to last.

statements.text: Women's football was popular with large crowds in the early twentieth century.

questions.passage: Sports fans have always believed that playing at home brings an advantage, and statistics broadly confirm their belief. Across many sports, home teams win more often than visiting teams, although the size of the effect varies considerably between sports and has declined in some over recent decades. Explaining why the advantage exists has proved more complicated. Travel fatigue and familiarity with local conditions play a part, but researchers have found that these factors account for only a small proportion of the effect. A more surprising explanation concerns referees. Several studies have suggested that officials, influenced perhaps unconsciously by the noise of a home crowd, tend to make slightly more decisions in favour of the home side. A remarkable opportunity to test this theory arose when many professional matches were played in empty stadiums during the pandemic. Analyses of those games found that the home advantage shrank noticeably in several leagues, and that the difference in the number of penalties and cards given to home and away teams largely disappeared. However, the results were not uniform: in some competitions, home teams continued to win more often, suggesting that crowds are an important factor but not the only one.

questions.passage: Climbing was once regarded as a dangerous pursuit for a small group of adventurers willing to travel to remote cliffs and mountains. The opening of indoor climbing centres in towns and cities has changed that image completely. Bouldering, a form of climbing on short walls without ropes, above thick protective mats, has proved especially popular, since it requires little equipment and can be learned quickly. Beginners can try a few routes on a first visit and see visible progress within weeks. Many centres have become social hubs, with cafés, yoga classes and evening sessions where people meet new friends. Climbing made its first appearance at the Olympic Games in 2021, which further boosted interest among young people. Physiotherapists note that the activity develops strength, flexibility and balance, and that solving the physical puzzles presented by each route also provides mental stimulation. Nevertheless, indoor climbing is not free from risk. Falls onto mats can still cause injuries, particularly to ankles and wrists, and overuse injuries to fingers are common among those who increase their training too quickly. Instructors recommend that newcomers learn how to fall safely and warm up properly before attempting difficult routes.

questions.explanation: Many new referees quit within two years, mainly because of abuse; body cameras appear to reduce abuse; officials say lasting change needs a cultural shift.
questions.passage: Every weekend, thousands of amateur football matches take place in parks and on school fields, but in many countries there are no longer enough referees to officiate them all. Local associations report that large numbers of new referees give up within their first two years, and some matches have had to be cancelled or supervised by volunteers with no formal qualifications. When asked why they quit, referees most frequently mention abuse from players, coaches and spectators, which ranges from insults shouted from the touchline to, in rare cases, physical assault. Young referees, some of them only teenagers, are particularly vulnerable. The low payments for officiating grassroots matches do little to compensate for such experiences. Associations have introduced a variety of measures in response. Some require teams to nominate a respect officer responsible for the behaviour of their supporters, while others have experimented with body cameras worn by referees, which appear to make abusive behaviour less likely. Mentoring schemes pairing new referees with experienced colleagues have also helped to reduce the number who drop out. Yet officials insist that lasting change depends on a cultural shift, in which players and spectators come to regard referees as essential participants rather than as obstacles to victory.

questions.passage: Insects are a regular part of the diet for an estimated two billion people, particularly in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America, yet in many Western countries the idea of eating them still provokes disgust. Advocates argue that this reluctance needs to be overcome. Compared with cattle, insects such as crickets and mealworms require far less land, water and feed to produce the same amount of protein, and they generate considerably lower greenhouse gas emissions. Some species can even be raised on food waste. Insects are also nutritious, containing high-quality protein, healthy fats and minerals such as iron and zinc. To make them more acceptable to cautious consumers, producers increasingly grind insects into flour, which can then be added to pasta, bread, energy bars and snacks without being visible. Despite these efforts, the market has grown more slowly than many investors predicted, and several start-ups have closed. Prices remain relatively high because production has not yet reached a large scale. Researchers who study food choices argue that information about environmental benefits is unlikely to change habits on its own. In their view, familiarity is crucial, and people are most likely to accept new foods when they are tasty, convenient and served by others they trust.

questions.passage: Walk down the aisle of any supermarket and you will find packaging covered in information: ingredients, nutritional values, health claims and, increasingly, colour-coded labels indicating whether a product is high or low in fat, sugar and salt. The aim of such labels is to help shoppers make healthier choices quickly, without needing to study detailed tables of figures. Evidence suggests that simple front-of-pack labels are more effective than complex ones, since most shoppers spend only a few seconds deciding what to buy. Some research has found that clear labelling leads consumers to choose slightly healthier products, although the effect on overall diet appears modest. Interestingly, labels may have a greater impact on manufacturers than on shoppers. Faced with the prospect of displaying a red warning on their best-selling products, a number of companies have quietly reformulated recipes to reduce sugar or salt. Food producers have not always welcomed these schemes, arguing that labels based on a standard portion can be misleading, for instance by classing olive oil or cheese alongside sweets and fizzy drinks. As a result, labelling systems differ from country to country, and in many places they remain voluntary rather than compulsory.

statements.text: Complex labels with detailed figures are the most effective.

questions.passage: Plant-based alternatives to meat have existed for decades, but early versions were often bland products aimed mainly at vegetarians. A new generation of burgers, sausages and minced products, developed with considerable scientific effort and investment, aims at a much larger market: people who enjoy meat but would like to eat less of it for environmental, health or ethical reasons. Some of these products imitate the taste, texture and even the appearance of beef remarkably closely. After an initial period of rapid growth, during which plant-based burgers appeared on the menus of major fast-food chains, sales in several countries began to level off or even decline. Analysts have suggested several explanations. Prices have generally remained higher than those of conventional meat, which makes the products less attractive when household budgets are tight. Some consumers have also expressed concern about the long lists of ingredients, regarding the products as highly processed. Nutritionists point out that being made from plants does not automatically make a product healthy, since some alternatives contain high levels of salt. Nevertheless, most experts expect the market to keep growing in the long term, particularly if improved technology allows producers to reduce costs.

questions.passage: Food fraud, the deliberate misrepresentation of food for financial gain, is as old as trade itself, but globalised supply chains have created new opportunities for it. Products that command high prices are particularly attractive targets. Extra virgin olive oil may be diluted with cheaper oils, honey can be mixed with sugar syrup, and expensive fish species are sometimes replaced with less valuable ones. Spices such as saffron, which is sold in tiny quantities at very high prices, have been bulked up with dyed plant material. In most cases, the main victims are consumers' wallets rather than their health, but fraud can occasionally be dangerous, as when undeclared ingredients cause allergic reactions. Detecting fraud has become a scientific discipline in its own right. Laboratories use techniques such as chemical fingerprinting and DNA analysis to establish a product's origin and composition, comparing samples with databases of authentic foods. Yet testing every product is impossible, and fraudsters continually adapt their methods to avoid detection. Experts therefore emphasise prevention, encouraging companies to know their suppliers, shorten supply chains where possible and be suspicious of prices that seem too good to be true. Consumers, too, can help by buying from trusted sources and reporting anything suspicious.

statements.text: Expensive foods are more likely to be targeted by fraudsters.
Food fraud usually causes serious harm to consumers' health.

questions.passage: Going to court is often imagined as an expensive and intimidating process involving lawyers in formal dress and lengthy proceedings. For many everyday disputes, however, a simpler route exists. Small claims procedures allow individuals and businesses to resolve disagreements involving relatively modest sums, such as a faulty product, an unpaid invoice or a deposit that a landlord refuses to return, without the costs of a full trial. The procedures are designed to be used without legal representation. Forms can usually be completed online, hearings are typically informal and held in an ordinary room rather than a traditional courtroom, and judges are expected to help both sides explain their case. In many systems, the party that loses is required to pay only limited costs, which reduces the financial risk of bringing a claim. Before a hearing takes place, both sides are frequently encouraged to try mediation, and a substantial proportion of disputes are settled at this stage. Despite these advantages, research suggests that many people with valid claims never use the system, either because they are unaware of it or because they assume that legal action is beyond their means. Consumer organisations argue that wider publicity could encourage more people to enforce their rights.

statements.text: Small claims procedures are intended for disputes involving large sums of money.
People can use the small claims process without hiring a lawyer.

Almost everyone with a valid claim makes use of the system.

questions.passage: In most legal systems, a fine for a particular offence is a fixed sum, the same for a wealthy executive as for a student or a pensioner. Critics argue that this approach is fundamentally unfair, since a penalty that represents a trivial expense for one person may cause genuine hardship for another. Several countries, particularly in northern Europe, have adopted a different model known as day fines. Under this system, the seriousness of an offence determines a number of units, while the value of each unit depends on the offender's daily income. As a result, two people who commit the same offence may pay vastly different amounts, and newspapers occasionally report speeding fines running into tens of thousands of euros for high earners. Supporters claim that day fines make punishment equally felt across society and that they deter wealthy offenders more effectively. Implementing the system, however, requires reliable information about people's incomes, which is easier in countries where tax records are accessible to the authorities. Some argue that it is also open to manipulation by those whose wealth comes from assets rather than salaries. Even so, interest in income-based fines has grown, with several cities and states examining whether they could reduce the burden of penalties on low-income households.

The value of a unit depends on how much the offender earns.

questions.passage: Surveys repeatedly show that a large proportion of adults have not made a will, even though most agree that it would be sensible to do so. Some people assume they do not own enough to make it worthwhile; others simply find it uncomfortable to think about their own death. Yet dying without a will can create considerable difficulties for those left behind. In such cases, property is distributed according to fixed legal rules, which may not reflect the deceased person's wishes. Unmarried partners, for example, may have no automatic right to inherit in some legal systems, however long the couple lived together, while relatives the deceased rarely saw may receive a share. Disputes between family members can also become more likely, and resolving them may take months or even years. Lawyers recommend reviewing a will after major life events such as marriage, divorce or the birth of a child, since an outdated document can cause almost as many problems as having none at all. Without clear instructions and access details, relatives may find it difficult, or even impossible, to retrieve them.
